requirements.req_text: Do the following: (a) Explain to your counselor the most likely hazards you may encounter while participating in whitewater activities, including branches and trees in water along a shore and stretching across the stream, rocks, hydraulics over ledges or low-head dams, strong wind, low water or air temperature, and thunder and lightning storms. Explain what you should do to anticipate, help prevent, mitigate, and respond to these hazards. (b) Review with your counselor the prevention, symptoms, and first-aid treatment for the following injuries or illnesses that could occur while participating in whitewater activities: cold-water shock; hypothermia; head, neck, and back injuries; heat-related illnesses; sunburn; dehydration; blisters; bruises; cuts; sprains and strains; shoulder dislocation; and submersion injuries. (c) Discuss with your counselor the Scouting America Safety Afloat policy and the American Whitewater safety guidelines, including the use of helmet and life jackets.

pamphlet_excerpts: Hazards, First Aid & Safety: Cool the victim immediately through immersion with cold packs in the groin area and armpits (p. 21).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 2: Increase the body's fluid level by having a conscious victim sip water (p. 21).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 3: Sunburn is an inflammation of the skin caused by toomuch exposure to the sun (p. 21).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 4: Shoulder dislocations are one of the most serious injuries associated with whitewater activities (p. 21).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): A shoulder becomes dislocatedwhen the ball at the end of the upper arm bone slips out of thesocket at the shoulder (p. 21).
Step 2 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): This can happen when a paddlerattempts a maneuver such as a high brace that involves reaching overhead to gain leverage with the paddle (p. 21).
Step 3 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Any stroke ormaneuver in which the arm is fully extended and then rotatedrearward so the elbow is behind the shoulder puts the shoulderjoint (p. 21).
Step 4 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): You can reduce the likelihood of such an injury by making sure you keep a slight bend inyour elbows and by keeping your grip or upper hand (p. 21).

pamphlet_excerpts: Ferrying Upstream and Downstream: Upstream (forward) ferries and downstream (back) ferries moveyou sideways across the current (p. 30).
Ferrying Upstream and Downstream Principle 2: In an upstream ferry, you faceupstream and paddle forward with your bow at an angle to thecurrent (p. 30).
Ferrying Upstream and Downstream Principle 3: You move across the current in the direction your bowis pointing (p. 30).
Ferrying Upstream and Downstream Principle 4: To perform a downstream ferry, you face downstream and backpaddle with your stern pointed upstream at anangle to the current (p. 30).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Ferrying Upstream and Downstream): You move across the current in the direction your stern is facing (p. 30).
Step 2 (Ferrying Upstream and Downstream): To perform a successful upstream ferry, begin by turningyour boat until it faces upstream (p. 30).
Step 3 (Ferrying Upstream and Downstream): As you start paddling, adjust the ferry angle, the angle of the boat compared to theupstream, to about 10 degrees (p. 30).
Step 4 (Ferrying Upstream and Downstream): If you are moving out of aneddy into the current, enter the current as if you were doing a peel out by exiting the eddy at about a 45-degree angle (p. 30).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Whitewater Swimmer and Boating Prerequisites): When you havelearned how to move in and out of eddies with confidence andease, you will have passed a major whitewater skills milestone (p. 56).

Step 3 (Whitewater Swimmer and Boating Prerequisites): The three importantcomponents of an eddy turn are angle, speed, and edge or tilt (p. 56).
Step 4 (Whitewater Swimmer and Boating Prerequisites): Aim thebow so it crosses the eddy line as close as possible to the top of the eddy (p. 56).

pamphlet_excerpts: Tandem Canoeist / Solo Canoeist / Solo Kayaker: In the peel out, note how both paddlers use their left knees to lean into and tilt the boat into the turn (p. 50).
Tandem Canoeist / Solo Canoeist / Solo Kayaker Principle 2: An offside peel out incorporates all the same features of the onside peel out except that the turning strokes are different (p. 50).
Tandem Canoeist / Solo Canoeist / Solo Kayaker Principle 3: For kayakers, the opposite paddle blade is used for the turningstroke (p. 50).
Tandem Canoeist / Solo Canoeist / Solo Kayaker Principle 4: After crossing the eddy line, solo canoeists can use avariety of turning strokes, including a forward sweep or crossbow draw (p. 50).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Tandem Canoeist / Solo Canoeist / Solo Kayaker): Tandem canoeists use a combination of a cross-bowdraw in the bow while the stern paddler does a low bracingreverse sweep or simply powers (p. 50).
Step 2 (Tandem Canoeist / Solo Canoeist / Solo Kayaker): The paddle shaft should be vertical and move in a path 2 to 3 feet long next to the side of the boat (p. 50).
Step 3 (Tandem Canoeist / Solo Canoeist / Solo Kayaker): Angle the blade at 45 degrees, as if you were spreading butter on a slice of bread, and move the paddle from side to side (p. 50).

requirements.req_text: Wearing a proper life jacket and being appropriately dressed for the weather and water conditions, perform the following skills in moving water in a properly equipped whitewater craft of your choice (tandem canoe, solo canoe, or solo kayak). If a tandem canoe is used, the skills must be demonstrated from both the bow and stern positions. (a) Launch and land. (b) Paddle forward in a straight line at least 10 boat lengths. (c) Backpaddle in a straight line at least five boat lengths. (d) Ferry upstream from both sides of the river. (e) Ferry downstream from both sides of the river. (f) Eddy turn from both sides of an eddy. (g) Peel out from both sides of an eddy.

pamphlet_excerpts: Wearing a proper life jacket: Upstream (forward) ferries and downstream (back) ferries moveyou sideways across the current (p. 46).
Wearing a proper life jacket Principle 2: In an upstream ferry, you faceupstream and paddle forward with your bow at an angle to thecurrent (p. 46).
Wearing a proper life jacket Principle 3: You move across the current in the direction your bowis pointing (p. 46).
Wearing a proper life jacket Principle 4: To perform a downstream ferry, you face downstream and backpaddle with your stern pointed upstream at anangle to the current (p. 46).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Wearing a proper life jacket): You move across the current in the direction your stern is facing (p. 46).
Step 2 (Wearing a proper life jacket): To perform a successful upstream ferry, begin by turningyour boat until it faces upstream (p. 46).
Step 3 (Wearing a proper life jacket): As you start paddling, adjust the ferry angle, the angle of the boat compared to theupstream, to about 10 degrees (p. 46).
Step 4 (Wearing a proper life jacket): If you are moving out of aneddy into the current, enter the current as if you were doing a peel out by exiting the eddy at about a 45-degree angle (p. 46).

pamphlet_excerpts: Using a Throw Rope to Rescue Others As you will recall, a throw rope is a floating rope that is stored in a throw bag (p. 71).
Using a Throw Rope to Rescue Others Principle 2: The rope will pay out neatly when the bagis tossed (p. 71).

Using a Throw Rope to Rescue Others Principle 3: A throw bag or a neatly coiled throw rope shouldalways be secured in your craft so that it will be handy in a rescue situation but is not an entrapment (p. 71).
Using a Throw Rope to Rescue Others Principle 4: Allow theremainder of the rope to stay in the bag (p. 71).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Using a Throw Rope to Rescue Others): Be sure that the mouth of the bag is onlyhalfway open (p. 71).
Step 2 (Using a Throw Rope to Rescue Others): Step 2, Get the attention of the person in the water by yelling, "Rope!" or giving a single blast of your whistle (p. 71).
Step 3 (Using a Throw Rope to Rescue Others): Step 3, Grasp or step on the freeend of the rope and toss the bag at the swimmer (p. 71).
Step 4 (Using a Throw Rope to Rescue Others): Ifyou miss, quickly restuff the bagor make arm-length coils of rope and try again (p. 71).

requirements.req_text: Participate in one or more whitewater trips using either a canoe or kayak on a Class I and/or Class II river. The trip(s) must involve at least six hours of paddling time. For each trip: (a) Help to prepare a written plan, specifying the route (put-ins and takeouts), schedule, equipment, safety precautions, and emergency procedures. (b) Determine local rules and obtain permission from landowners and land managers in advance. (c) Explain what steps have been taken to comply with Scouting America Safety Afloat and the American Whitewater safety guidelines. (d) Show how to protect personal and group equipment from water and how to load and secure the containers in boats to be used in the trip. Execute the plans with other paddlers. (e) Explain to your counselor how well your plans worked for each trip taken.
